synthesis.headline: The week-long cutoff hands off: a maturing southern-Plains trough slides toward a Gulf/Southeast flood regime while the northern stream takes charge — and the western ridge that looked finished yesterday reloads in week two
synthesis.narrative:
The organizing story is a two-stream handoff. The amplified, blocked couplet Tlaloc has tracked all week is now entering its exit phase: at 500 mb the once-discrete interior-West cutoff has broadened into a deep central-US longwave trough, nearly cut off with a height minimum of roughly 540-546 dam over the southern Plains and a slight negative (NW-SE) tilt from the northern Rockies southeast. That is the same slow, pivoting system in roughly its fourth day, still walled off enough to creep rather than sweep. But the northern stream has woken up around it: a vigorous 1002-1004 mb surface cyclone has come onshore over the north-central Rockies/northern Great Basin — the Pacific disturbance yesterday's analysis flagged as the first to erode the ridge — trailing a cold front through the central Plains with the chart's tightest pressure gradient (and strongest winds) from the northern Plains south through the central Rockies. Behind it, a strong 1026 mb cold high over the PNW/northern Rockies and a 1024 mb center over the upper Midwest mark the fall airmass beginning to push south, reinforced from the north by a formidable 1039 hPa high over the Keewatin/western Hudson Bay region on the Canadian analysis.

Focal points, in order of consequence: first, heavy rain. WPC carries a Moderate Risk for excessive rainfall today over the Southern Plains as Gulf moisture pools ahead of the front, with flash-flood and burn-scar debris-flow concern, and a Slight Risk reaching the Central Plains, mid-Mississippi Valley and Great Lakes. Severe weather is a secondary note today — SPC keeps organized potential low, cloud cover and poor lapse rates capping destabilization, so repetitive heavy rain is the real threat and only gusty storms with small hail are likely near the mid-level low in the Panhandle/southern Kansas. Second, the Mid-Atlantic/southern New England coast, where the Air Mass RGB shows a tight airmass boundary with curving cirrus filaments consistent with a coastal cyclone or occlusion, with the broad 1021-1022 mb offshore high leaving a slack gradient down the seaboard. Third, a NE-SW convective band from Louisiana/Mississippi toward the Carolinas along the trailing boundary, plus a deep-convective cluster over the central Gulf — tropical-moisture players feeding the developing South/Southeast rain focus, not named threats (NHC expects no Atlantic development for seven days).

The upper pattern ties it together and sets up the week. The ridge over the Pacific Northwest and into southern Canada still reaches the upper 570s to near 580 dam, a genuinely amplified couplet with the trough to its east, and the implied jet wraps cyclonically from the Southwest northeastward toward the Great Lakes at 60-70+ kt. The Air Mass RGB confirms the mechanism: a dry streamer descending the eastern Rockies and High Plains through Texas and curving toward the Gulf marks the trough's western flank, its leading edge the ascent corridor into the moist plume driving the Southern Plains rain; the full-disk view shows a sharp color boundary across Canada marking the leading edge of the polar airmass now sagging south. Where today departs from yesterday's read is the medium range. Yesterday Tlaloc called the northern ridge genuinely transitioning — contracting and retreating toward the Southwest, with no rebuild. Today's ensemble pair tells a more nuanced story, and it matters to say so. The 6-10 day (Oct 6-10) does flatten the West: near-zero height anomalies, the zero line pulled back to the interior West near 110-115W, a progressive near-zonal CONUS flow, and the dominant positive anomaly displaced east to a +9 to +12 dam ridge over/west of Hudson Bay. But the 8-14 day (Oct 8-14) swings the other way — a strong +90 m ridge rebuilds over the Pacific Northwest, BC coast and northern Rockies (ridge core anchored there, not retreated to the Southwest), while central Canada/Hudson Bay flips from that 6-10 day ridge to a deep trough. Read as a pair, this looks less like a clean regime change and more like a temporary progressive flattening — the train of northern-stream fronts passing through — followed by re-amplification of a northern-tier western ridge. WPC's extended discussion supports that framing explicitly, describing northern-stream amplification over time behind the progressive fronts. The honest caveat: the two panels disagree on where the dominant ridge lives (Hudson Bay at 6-10, PNW at 8-14), so confidence in the week-2 placement is only moderate, but the signal is regeneration of western ridging, not its demise.
synthesis.climate_context: The basin behavior is textbook moderate-to-strong El Niño: the ONI table, though lagging at its labeled value, climbs to about +1.8 by JJA 2026, placing early October squarely in El Niño territory, and the hemispheric tropics fit that state — a hyperactive East Pacific (Hurricane Rachel south of Baja California Sur, Tropical Storm Nolo west of Hawaii, Tropical Depression Nineteen-E, and a low south of southern Mexico at 70% odds through seven days) against a suppressed Atlantic with no development expected. The North American Monsoon is in its fading late-season phase but still contributes the Pacific-and-Gulf moisture overlap feeding the Southwest-to-South-Central and now South/Southeast rains. Severe-weather season is settling into its expected late-season, ridge-periphery mode rather than a deep-Plains outbreak, consistent with today's capped, heavy-rain-dominated setup. Teleconnection indices carry only cross-check weight and lag the height field: the modestly negative PNA (-0.34) is consistent with the absence of a durable western ridge at the moment, which squares with the 6-10 day flattening more than the week-2 rebuild; the sharply negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.01) fits the high-latitude blocking tendency over Hudson Bay/the Arctic. These should not be leaned on hard, and the templated "summer" framing in the index notes should be read as October reality.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and is not monitoring an organized convective threat. The sharpest local signal today is the Southern Plains flash-flood threat, including debris-flow potential over recent burn scars within the Moderate Risk footprint, with repetitive heavy rain rather than organized severe the dominant hazard. On the warm side of the pattern, hazardous heat builds for southern California and the Desert Southwest into the weekend and early next week under the Southwest ridge, with highs into the 90s and low 100s. In Canada, the strong Keewatin high and the frontal low to its south combine for a northerly-to-northwesterly post-frontal airmass push into the Prairie provinces and Ontario; a deep 962 hPa low sits near Greenland/Baffin Bay, outside populated areas. Off western Mexico, Hurricane Rachel (roughly 85-105 kt) remains the standout Eastern Pacific system.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 1 October 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a vigorous cyclone over the north-central Rockies/northern Great Basin area with a central pressure near 1002-1004 mb, accompanied by a cold front trailing southward through the central Plains and a warm front extending northeast toward the Great Lakes; a second, weaker low near 1002 mb sits over the southern Plains, with a separate frontal boundary curving through the Gulf Coast region. The dominant anticyclone is a strong 1026 mb high centered over the Pacific Northwest/northern Rockies, with another high near 1024 mb over the upper Midwest and a 1022-1021 mb high parked off the mid-Atlantic coast, the latter creating a broadly slack gradient over the eastern seaboard. The tightest pressure gradient on the chart is along and ahead of the cold front from the northern Plains southward through the central Rockies, where isobars are most compressed, implying the strongest surface winds in that corridor. Moisture focus is clearest along the warm sector ahead of the trailing cold front over the central and southern Plains, where dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s°F are depicted, and along the Gulf Coast frontal boundary where similarly high dewpoints and the front's position together favor organized lift. Hurricane Rachel's annotation in the lower Gulf of California region with a max wind notation near 85-105 kt represents the only tropical system on the chart, though its isobaric signature is not clearly resolved at this scale.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This is a CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Thursday 01 October 2026, on a polar stereographic projection whose upper portions cover the high Arctic and Canadian Archipelago rather than the populated south. The dominant feature over Canada itself is a strong 1039 hPa high centered over what appears to be the western Hudson Bay or Keewatin district region, with tightly packed isobars on its eastern flank implying a substantial pressure gradient toward a 962 hPa low visible in the upper-right quadrant of the chart, which given the projection geometry places it over or near Greenland or Baffin Bay rather than over any province. Across southern Canada the pressure pattern is relatively slack, with a 1021 hPa high over what appears to be the southern Prairies or northern Great Plains area and a weak low near 1008 hPa in the central part of the domain that, by the frontal symbols attached, is drawing a cold front southward and eastward across what is likely the Great Lakes or upper Midwest border region. The remnants of Tropical Depression Surigae are labeled at 33.2N 140.7E in the western Pacific, well outside the Canadian domain and of no direct relevance here. The tightest gradient affecting southern Canadian populated areas appears to be between the strong high over the Keewatin and the frontal low to its south, suggesting a northerly to northwesterly post-frontal airmass push into the Prairie provinces and Ontario, though the exact position of the frontal boundary relative to specific provinces is difficult to resolve precisely at this chart scale.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb, the dominant feature is a deep longwave trough over the central United States, with the height minimum appearing near the southern Plains at roughly 540-546 dam, and closed contours visible in that region suggesting a cutoff or nearly cutoff low rather than an open trough still embedded in the westerlies. The trough axis tilts slightly negatively (northwest to southeast) from the northern Rockies into the southern Plains, which is consistent with an amplifying or recently amplified pattern rather than a progressive one. A pronounced ridge occupies the Pacific Northwest and into southern Canada, with heights reaching into the upper 570s to near 580 dam over that sector, and the sharpness of the ridge-trough couplet indicates substantial meridional amplitude. The implied jet corridor wraps cyclonically around the trough, with wind speeds in the color shading suggesting a streak of 60-70+ knots arcing from the Southwest northeastward toward the Great Lakes, though precise jet axis placement is uncertain at the eastern flank. A separate weak ridge is analyzed along the Atlantic seaboard with a high center marked near the Southeast coast; flow across the eastern third of the country appears broadly anticyclonic and relatively slack, suggesting the overall pattern is retrogressive or blocked rather than progressive, with the cutoff low likely to persist and pivot rather than translate quickly downstream.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This 1 October 2026 13:31Z AirMass RGB shows a broad swath of red-orange dry upper-tropospheric air dominating the central and northern Plains eastward through the Ohio Valley, consistent with the subsiding air on the anticyclonic side of the mid-latitude flow rather than a stratospheric intrusion. A sharper, more elongated dry streamer descends southward along the eastern Rockies and High Plains through Texas, curving cyclonically toward the Gulf Coast, which is the geometry expected on the western and equatorward flank of a trough or shortwave; the boundary between this streamer and the moist green air to its east marks the implied jet corridor. Organized deep convection, indicated by bright white cold cloud tops, is present in two areas: a cluster over the central Gulf of Mexico and another along a NE-SW-oriented band stretching from roughly Louisiana and Mississippi northeastward toward the Carolinas, consistent with a trailing frontal or convective boundary. The Mid-Atlantic and southern New England coastline shows a tight airmass boundary with curving cirrus filaments, suggesting a coastal cyclone or occlusion in progress there. A separate intense convective center with very bright tops is visible near the lower-left corner of the image, over or near the eastern Pacific just off the Mexican coast, well outside the continental domain.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: At 1320Z on 1 October 2026, the GOES-19 AirMass RGB shows a broad green swath of tropical moist air extending from the eastern Pacific across Central America and into the western Amazon basin, with embedded clusters of bright white deep convective tops scattered from southern Mexico southward along the ITCZ and over the Colombian and Peruvian Andes foothills. A well-organized curved cloud mass with a tight cold-top signature is visible off the Mexican Pacific coast, consistent with a tropical cyclone or strong tropical wave at that position. Over the Southern Ocean southeast of southern South America, two cyclonic swirls are apparent, with the more westward one displaying a compact orange-red dry intrusion wrapping into its core on the poleward side, the geometry and saturation of which are consistent with a stratospheric intrusion associated with that extratropical system. Across Canada and the Arctic limb, a sharp color boundary separates the dark blue cold upper-tropospheric air of the high latitudes from the more orange mid-tropospheric air over the central and western United States, marking an airmass boundary that implies the leading edge of a polar airmass. The South Atlantic and eastern Pacific subtropical regions are dominated by broad, relatively uniform orange-red hues consistent with dry, subsident air under the respective subtropical highs, without the compact elongated structure that would suggest stratospheric intrusion.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a strong above-normal signal across the entire western contiguous US, with the highest probabilities, 90-100 percent, centered over southern California and the immediate interior, grading eastward through 70-80 and 60-70 percent tiers across the Rockies and High Plains before fading to near-normal across the middle Mississippi Valley and most of the Southeast. A competing below-normal signal, at 50-60 percent probability, covers the northeastern states from roughly Maine through New Jersey and into interior New England, suggesting a trough or cool airmass position favored in that corner of the domain. Southern Florida stands apart from the rest of the East with a 33-40 percent above-normal lean, likely reflecting persistent subtropical warmth rather than the same ridge driving the West. In Alaska, the southern coastal arc carries 80-90 percent above-normal probabilities while interior and northern areas are near-normal and the far western tip leans above; the Big Island of Hawaii shows an above-normal lean while the northwestern Hawaiian chain reads near-normal to below. The steep east-west probability gradient across the contiguous US, with the most confident warm signal pinned to the Pacific Coast and weakening steadily eastward, is consistent with a ridge axis implied to be anchored near or just off the West Coast persisting into the 6-10 day window, though the gradual erosion of the signal across the central US and the opposing below-normal signal in the Northeast suggest the pattern may be relaxing or that a downstream trough is already embedded in the medium-range solution.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 6-10 October 2026, with heights in dam (solid green, 60 dam intervals) and anomalies in dam (dashed, red positive, blue negative).

The dominant positive anomaly center sits over or just west of Hudson Bay and the eastern Canadian Arctic, where red dashed contours reach roughly +9 to +12 dam, indicating a pronounced above-normal ridge anchored well into central Canada. Over the western contiguous United States and the eastern Pacific, the anomaly field shows weakly positive or near-zero values: the zero-anomaly line appears to run roughly along the 110-115°W longitude band through the interior West, meaning the western ridge is not strongly amplified in the anomaly sense and positive anomalies do not extend robustly to the Pacific coast. A negative anomaly center is evident over the north-central Pacific, with blue dashed contours suggesting departures on the order of -6 to -9 dam, and a secondary negative center is implied over Alaska and the Bering Sea region. The height pattern shows a broad trough axis oriented roughly north-south across Alaska and the northeastern Pacific, a ridge axis arcing from the southwestern United States northeastward into Hudson Bay, and another trough axis suggested near or east of Greenland; the overall contour spacing across the mid-latitudes of the contiguous United States is relatively tight and zonally oriented, consistent with a largely progressive, near-zonal flow regime dominating the lower 48 rather than a strongly amplified western ridge pattern.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a CPC 8-14 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly prognostic valid 8-14 October 2026, made 30 September 2026. The green solid contours are heights in meters at 60 m intervals, and the dashed contours are anomalies; labeled height values near the ridge center over the south-central United States read around 582-588 dam, consistent with a strong late-season ridge. The most prominent positive anomaly center, labeled near +90 on the dashed contours, sits over the Pacific coast and interior of British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest, indicating a well-above-normal ridge axis that extends from roughly the BC coast into the northern Rockies; a second positive lobe of similar magnitude appears far to the east over the western Atlantic. The ridge axis in the height field runs roughly from the southwest United States northward through the Rockies into western Canada, meaning the ridge core has not retreated to the southwest but instead remains anchored over the northern Rockies and Pacific Northwest, which is the more amplified outcome. A broad negative anomaly region centered near -90 to -30 is implied across central Canada into Hudson Bay, consistent with a trough positioned over that region, while the southern United States sits beneath relatively flat but above-normal heights. At this lead time the ensemble mean will smooth extremes, so the depicted anomaly pattern likely understates what individual solutions show, but the dominant signal is clearly a ridge over the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies flanked by downstream troughing over central Canada.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Moderate Risk of excessive rainfall Thursday over Southern Plains as Gulf moisture pools ahead of a frontal system, with numerous flash flooding and potential debris flows in recently burned areas. Slight Risk extends to Central Plains, Middle Mississippi Valley, and Great Lakes Thursday. Rain develops Friday along and ahead of the front from Northeast to Ohio Valley, with Slight Risk continuing over Southern Plains for localized flash flooding. Pacific Northwest frontal system moves eastward, reaching Northern Plains by Saturday with rain over Upper Mississippi Valley. Saturday brings Slight Risk for Central Gulf Coast, Lower Mississippi Valley, and Southern Appalachians.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Low organized severe potential today. Strong storms with gusty winds possible across Kansas southward through central and southern Texas. Extensive convection from eastern Oklahoma into north Texas and the Hill Country/Edwards Plateau will shift gradually eastward, supported by warm advection ahead of a surface low and cold front. Cloud cover and poor lapse rates limit destabilization; repetitive locally heavy rainfall is the main concern. In southern Kansas, Texas Panhandle, and northern Oklahoma near the mid-level low, cloud breaks and heating may allow stronger updrafts this afternoon with gusty winds and small hail possible. Limited funnel potential exists near boundaries, though suboptimal mid-level temperatures and increasingly southward-progressive cold front reduce this threat. Low-level winds weaken throughout the day.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions currently issued. Storm Prediction Center is not actively monitoring any organized convective threat at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next seven days.

East Pacific: Three active systems under advisories—Tropical Storm Nolo west of Hawaii, Hurricane Rachel south of Baja California Sur, and Tropical Depression Nineteen-E. An area of low pressure south of southern Mexico could develop late this weekend or early next week with favorable conditions for gradual development. Formation likelihood is near zero percent through 48 hours but rises to 70 percent through seven days as the system moves slowly west-northwestward to northwestward.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows transition from weak La Niña conditions (NDJ 2025 at -0.60 anomaly) toward El Niño. Anomalies remain slightly negative through early 2026, crossing into positive territory by spring. By summer 2026 (JJA), the index reaches +1.80 anomaly, indicating moderate El Niño development. The warming trend accelerates notably from April onward, with the strongest anomalies appearing in late boreal summer.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains modestly negative (-0.34, 7-day mean -0.58), showing little change; this weak signal offers minimal directional support in summer. AO has swung positive (+0.53) after several days of negative values, now neutral on average; negative AO phases favor Arctic blocking. NAO has fallen notably to -0.66 with a 7-day mean of -1.01, down 0.49 from the prior week—this negative trend is most significant, potentially affecting whether eastern North American troughs can decouple and escape northeastward. All indices are relatively weak; summer teleconnections carry reduced canonical weight.
